notes.title: Chapter map: OO design principles

headings.text: 📋 At a glance: the tell → the item

notes.html:
The principles actually applied in a 45–90 minute object-design round. Items 7 and 10 carry the section; 11 → 9 → 8 is the diagnosis chain; 12 → 13 are the mechanics. Read each arrow as a sentence: open/closed is made possible by encapsulation of invariants.

Green = 🔴 CORE, blue = 🟡 SUPPORTING, yellow = 🟢 BREADTH, grey = another section (dashed edges).

Reading order:07 open/closed10 encapsulation of invariants11 anemic domain model09 tell, don't ask08 composition over inheritance12 interface segregation13 constructor injection06 SOLID, a violation each

Owners

Idea Owner note
One three-line violation per SOLID letter, for "which principle does this break?" 06
"Now add X" is a new class or an edit: the rubric, and the recovery line when it is an edit 07
Delegate and inject in place of a deep extends chain 08
a.getB().getC().do() as a smell; behaviour moves to the data 09
No public setters on state that must stay consistent; intent methods 10
Getter-and-setter classes with logic in a service; the Spring tension 11
PricingStrategy, NotificationChannel, AllocationPolicy as the knobs follow-ups turn 12
No new inside business classes; testability as a scored dimension 13
What each SOLID principle means, explained with Java and Python SOLID, not these notes
What encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism are OOP: four pillars, not these notes
When not to add a seam DRY, KISS, YAGNI, not these notes
The patterns these principles turn into §3 design patterns, not these notes

Decision trees

No decision tree: these are checks you run together, not alternatives. The lookup below maps what you see to the item.

At a glance: the tell → the item

What you see Item The fix
a follow-up feature needs an edit to an if / switch 07 pull what varies behind a strategy
a public setter on status, balance or count 10 an intent method that enforces the rule
classes of getters and setters; rules live in a Service 11 move the transition onto the entity
a chain of getters reaching through objects 09 ask the first object to do it
a four-level extends chain 08 hold the varying part in a field
one interface that some implementers can't honour 12, 06 several small interfaces
new or a static singleton inside business logic 13 pass it through the constructor

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: an invariant with one owner can be extended, locked and refactored; an invariant scattered across callers can't.
  • The two most-confused pairs: open/closed vs over-engineering (07 against pattern overuse) · dependency inversion vs dependency injection (owned by SOLID; applied in 13).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: the table above, and item 07's recovery line.
  • Cross-section links: explained from first principles in §0 foundations; item 10's intent method is the unit you lock in §4; item 13 makes the tests in §5 possible.

notes.title: SOLID, With a Concrete Violation for Each
notes.html:
Reference Links

  • The principles restated by their author, with what they're actually for — Robert C. Martin: Solid Relevance

Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What form does the question take? "Which principle does this violate?" — never "define SRP."
The two that actually bite in LLD? OCP and DIP. LSP and ISP are asked about, rarely designed against.
LSP's canonical violation? Square extends Rectangle: setWidth breaks the rectangle's contract.
ISP's canonical violation? A fat interface where implementers throw UnsupportedOperationException.
DIP in one line? Depend on the abstraction; the concrete class is injected, never new-ed inside.

The 30-Second Answer

Memorise one three-line violation per letter, not five definitions. The question in an LLD round is always diagnostic — the interviewer shows you code, or points at your own, and asks which principle it breaks. Definitions don't answer that; recognisable shapes do.

The Five, With Their Shapes

S — Single Responsibility. Violation: a Booking class that also formats the confirmation email and writes the audit log. The tell is "and" in the class description. Fix: the class keeps the decision, the formatting moves out.

class Booking { void confirm(); String toEmailHtml(); void writeAuditLog(); }  // three reasons to change

O — Open/Closed. Violation: adding weekend pricing means editing price(). The tell is a switch or an if-chain over a type or category. Fix: Strategy. This is the one the round is actually scored on (→ item 7).

if (day == SATURDAY) p = p.multiply(WEEKEND);   // next rule edits this method

L — Liskov Substitution. Violation: Square extends Rectangle, overriding setWidth to also set the height. Any code written against Rectangle — "set width to 5, set height to 4, expect area 20" — breaks when handed a Square. The subtype narrowed a contract the supertype promised. Fix: they aren't a subtype relationship; both are Shape with an area().

class Square extends Rectangle {
    @Override void setWidth(int w)  { super.setWidth(w); super.setHeight(w); }   // surprise
}

I — Interface Segregation. Violation: one Vehicle interface with chargeBattery() and refuel(), so PetrolCar throws UnsupportedOperationException on one and ElectricCar on the other. The tell is that exception. Fix: two interfaces, implemented as applicable.

class PetrolCar implements Vehicle {
    public void chargeBattery() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }   // the smell
}

D — Dependency Inversion. Violation: BookingService calls new StripeGateway() inside confirm(). It can't be tested, and a second provider means editing the service. Fix: constructor-inject a PaymentGateway (→ item 13).

class BookingService { void confirm() { new StripeGateway().charge(...); } }   // untestable, closed

Why It Decides the Round

Only two of the five change what you build. OCP is the scoring rubric itself — the follow-up feature is either a new class or an edit, and that's decided by whether you put an interface on the axis that moved. DIP is what makes the design testable, and testability is a scored dimension.

The other three are recognition knowledge. You should be able to name the violation instantly when shown one, and you should not be spending design minutes on ISP in a parking-lot problem.

Failure Mode

Reciting definitions. "Single Responsibility means a class should have one reason to change" answers a question nobody asked. The response wanted is "that's SRP — this class both decides and formats."

Designing against all five. In forty-five minutes, closed-by-default plus interfaces on the one or two moving axes is the correct amount. Prophylactic ISP is speculative generality.

Connections

  • Next: 07-open-closed-as-the-scoring-rubric.md — the letter that carries the weight.
  • DIP in practice: 13-constructor-dependency-injection.md
  • Patterns: ../03-design-patterns/14-strategy.md — the OCP fix.

notes.title: Open/Closed as the Scoring Rubric
notes.html:
Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is the round actually scoring? Whether the named follow-up feature is a new class rather than an edit.
The test, in one sentence? If adding X requires editing an existing if/switch, the design is wrong on that axis.
When did the interviewer choose X? Before you walked in. Your first ten minutes are a bet on which axis.
The four axes that cover almost everything? Policy (Strategy), lifecycle (State), creation by type (Factory), integration (Adapter).
What makes an extension point justified? You can name the concrete future requirement it absorbs.

The 30-Second Answer

Nearly every LLD follow-up is "now add feature X." The design is scored by what adding X costs: a new class implementing an existing interface is a pass; an edit to a method you already wrote is a fail on that axis. So the whole first ten minutes are about guessing which axis X sits on and putting an interface there — and the clarifying questions (item 1) are how you narrow the guess.

Why It's The Rubric

Interviewers don't score "is this good code" — that's unfalsifiable in forty-five minutes. They score a concrete event: they name a feature, you add it, and they watch what happens to the existing code. That's repeatable across candidates, which is why it's the rubric.

Which means the design decisions that matter are the ones that survive contact with that event, and everything else — naming, layering aesthetics, how many patterns you named — is noise around it.

The corollary that people miss: closed is the default. OCP does not say "make everything extensible." An interface with one implementation and no named future requirement costs a reader real effort and buys nothing; interviewers call it speculative generality, and applying it uniformly is the pattern-overuse failure (→ item 26). Open along the axis that will move, closed everywhere else.

The Four Axes

Axis Tell that you need it Pattern Typical follow-up
Policy pricing, scheduling, matching, allocation, eviction Strategy "now add surge pricing"
Lifecycle nested if on a status field State "what if it's cancelled mid-flight?"
Creation by type switch on an enum to build something Factory "now support motorbikes"
Integration a third-party name inside domain code Adapter "now support a second payment provider"

Three or four extension points is what a 60-minute round affords. Spending them on the axes the problem statement hints at is judgment; spending them uniformly is overuse; spending none is the mid-level design.

In Practice

The moment the follow-up lands is the scoring event, and there's a right way to handle it:

Them: "Now add weekend pricing." You: "That's a new PricingRule — WeekendMultiplier — added to the engine's list. Nothing in PricingEngine changes." (writes eight lines)

And when it lands on an axis you didn't anticipate, honesty beats quiet surgery:

Them: "Now the elevator has an express mode that skips floors 2–10." You: "My dispatch is a strategy, so the selection is fine — but I put the stop-decision inline in Elevator.step(), so this would edit that method. I'd pull the stop predicate out into the strategy too. Want me to do that refactor, or note it and move on?"

Naming your own design's limit scores better than editing four methods while saying nothing.

Failure Mode

A switch on an enum inside business logic. The single most reliable indicator of a closed design, and the first thing a follow-up will hit.

Abstracting everything. Six interfaces on a parking lot is a negative signal, not a senior one.

Silently editing. If the follow-up forces a change to existing code, say so. The interviewer already knows.

Connections

  • Previous: 06-solid-with-a-violation-each.md
  • Next: 08-composition-over-inheritance.md
  • The fix: ../03-design-patterns/14-strategy.md · ../03-design-patterns/18-state.md
  • The limit: ../03-design-patterns/26-pattern-overuse.md

notes.title: Composition Over Inheritance
notes.html:
Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The tell of a mid-level design? A four-level extends chain.
Why do hierarchies break? They encode one classification axis. The second requirement adds a second axis, and you get a combinatorial explosion.
What replaces it? Delegation to an injected collaborator; the "type" becomes a field, not a subclass.
When is inheritance right? A genuine is-a with a stable, single axis and no behaviour variation the subtype must contradict (→ LSP).

The 30-Second Answer

Inheritance commits you to one classification axis at design time. The second requirement almost always introduces a second axis, and subclasses multiply as their product — ElectricLargeVehicle, PetrolLargeVehicle, ElectricSmallVehicle. Composition turns each axis into a field you can vary independently, which is why the follow-up feature stays additive.

Why It Decides the Round

The combinatorial explosion is the argument, and it's worth being able to state numerically. Vehicles classified by size (small/medium/large) and fuel (petrol/electric/hybrid) is nine subclasses under inheritance and two fields under composition. Add a third axis — ownership, say — and it's twenty-seven versus three.

The second argument is that inheritance couples you to a behaviour you may need to contradict, which is where LSP violations come from (→ item 6). A subclass that overrides a method to do something the supertype's callers don't expect has broken code it never saw. A delegate can't, because nobody wrote code against the delegate expecting the outer class's semantics.

In Practice

// ❌ One axis baked in. Adding "fuel type" doubles the hierarchy.
abstract class Vehicle {}
class Car extends Vehicle {}
class LargeCar extends Car {}
class LargeElectricCar extends LargeCar {}     // ← four levels, and this is only two axes

// ✅ Axes become fields. Each varies independently; a new fuel type is a new enum constant.
public final class Vehicle {
    private final VehicleSize size;          // SMALL / MEDIUM / LARGE  → spot fitting
    private final FuelType fuel;             // PETROL / ELECTRIC       → charging surcharge
    private final LicensePlate plate;

    public boolean fitsIn(ParkingSpot spot) { return spot.accommodates(size); }
    public Money surcharge(FeeSchedule fees) { return fees.forFuel(fuel); }
}

The parking-lot version of this is a common trap: Vehicle → Car → Motorbike → Truck looks natural until the follow-up is "handle EVs, which need a charging spot," and the natural place to put that is a second axis. If size and fuel are fields, EV support is a new enum constant plus a FeeSchedule entry. If they're subclasses, it's a new branch of the tree crossed with the existing one.

One place inheritance is still right: a small, closed set of behaviours that genuinely differ and never need to combine — PricingRule implementations, State implementations, chess Piece movement rules. That's inheritance used for polymorphic dispatch, one level deep, which is a different thing from inheritance used for classification.

Failure Mode

Building the hierarchy in minute five because the nouns extraction (item 3) produced Car, Truck, Motorbike and they look like an obvious tree. Ask first whether anything varies along a second axis.

Protected fields. A subclass reaching into the parent's state is the coupling that makes hierarchies impossible to change later.

Overcorrecting. One level of interface + implementations is the right shape for Strategy and State. "Composition over inheritance" isn't "never use implements."

Connections

  • Previous: 07-open-closed-as-the-scoring-rubric.md
  • Next: 09-law-of-demeter-tell-dont-ask.md
  • Related: 06-solid-with-a-violation-each.md — LSP is the formal version of this argument.
  • Worked: ../../07-Design-problems/parking-lot.md — the vehicle hierarchy trap.

notes.title: Law of Demeter / Tell-Don't-Ask
notes.html:
Reference Links

  • The principle, and why it's about bundling data with behaviour — Martin Fowler: Tell Don't Ask

Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The shape of the smell? a.getB().getC().doThing() — a train wreck.
What's wrong with it? The caller now depends on B's internals and C's. Either can break it.
Tell-don't-ask in one line? Don't pull data out to decide; hand the decision to the object that owns the data.
Where does this bite in LLD? It's the mechanism by which the anemic model spreads (→ item 11).

The 30-Second Answer

booking.getShow().getScreen().getTheatre().getName() couples the caller to three classes it never asked for; a change in any of them breaks it. The fix is not a helper method that hides the chain — it's moving the behaviour to where the data lives, so the caller says what it wants rather than reaching for what it needs.

Why It Matters

It's the transmission mechanism for the anemic domain model. Once a class exposes getters for its internals, every caller that needs a decision made about that state makes it itself — and the rule ends up implemented in five places, each of which is a place it can be got wrong. Fowler's framing is the useful one: the point of bundling data with functions is that the function is the only thing that has to know the data's shape.

In an LLD round it shows up as a service that reads three fields off an entity, evaluates a condition, and writes a fourth field back. That's a method on the entity.

In Practice

// ❌ Ask: the caller pulls state out, decides, writes back. The rule lives here now.
if (seat.getStatus() == HELD
        && seat.getHeldBy().equals(userId)
        && Instant.now().isBefore(seat.getHoldExpiresAt())) {
    seat.setStatus(BOOKED);
} else {
    throw new IllegalStateException();
}

// ✅ Tell: the object that owns the state owns the transition.
seat.confirm(userId, clock);      // throws HoldExpiredException / NotTheHolderException

The second version is four fewer getters, one fewer setter, and the rule now has exactly one home — which is also what makes the State-pattern follow-up (→ item 18) easy rather than a rewrite.

The honest limit. Demeter is a heuristic, not a law. Chains through value objects and collections are usually fine — order.total().amount().compareTo(...) isn't a coupling problem because Money has no lifecycle to break. And behaviour that genuinely spans entities — debt simplification across a Splitwise graph, dispatch across a bank of elevators — belongs in a service or domain service, not bolted onto one entity. Tell-don't-ask is about invariants, not about emptying the service layer.

Failure Mode

Hiding the chain instead of moving the behaviour. booking.getTheatreName() that internally does getShow().getScreen().getTheatre().getName() is the same coupling with a nicer face — though it is at least one place to fix instead of many.

Applying it to value objects. Wrapping every Money access in a delegating method is ceremony with no bug prevented.

Connections

  • Previous: 08-composition-over-inheritance.md
  • Next: 10-encapsulation-of-invariants.md — the same idea, stated as an ownership rule.
  • Consequence of ignoring it: 11-anemic-domain-model.md

notes.title: Encapsulation of Invariants
notes.html:
Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The rule? No public setters on state that must stay consistent.
What replaces them? Intent methods named after the transition — reserve(), release(), confirm().
What is an invariant? A statement that must be true of the object at every observable moment.
Where should validity be established? The constructor. An object that exists is an object that is valid.
The test question? "Can a caller put this object into an illegal state?" If yes, the invariant has no owner.

The 30-Second Answer

If a field can only change in specific ways, the only way to change it should be a method named after one of those ways. setStatus(BOOKED) lets any caller skip the rules; confirm(userId, clock) enforces them in one place. The invariant then has an owner, and the number of places it can be violated drops from every caller to one method.

Why It Decides the Round

It's the concrete, code-level version of everything in items 9 and 11, and it's the difference an interviewer can see in five seconds of reading. A class with getStatus/setStatus has told them the state machine lives somewhere else; a class with hold/confirm/release and no setter has told them it lives here.

It's also load-bearing for the concurrency follow-up. You cannot make a transition atomic if the transition isn't a method — locking around setStatus protects the write but not the check that should have preceded it. The intent method is the unit you put the lock or the compute around (→ items 27, 30).

In Practice

public final class ShowSeat {
    private Status status = Status.AVAILABLE;
    private UserId heldBy;
    private Instant holdExpiresAt;

    // Every legal transition is a method. There is no other way in.
    public void hold(UserId user, Duration ttl, Clock clock) {
        if (status != Status.AVAILABLE && !isHoldExpired(clock))
            throw new SeatUnavailableException(status);
        this.status = Status.HELD;
        this.heldBy = user;
        this.holdExpiresAt = clock.instant().plus(ttl);
    }

    public void confirm(UserId user, Clock clock) {
        if (status != Status.HELD)        throw new SeatUnavailableException(status);
        if (!heldBy.equals(user))         throw new NotTheHolderException(user);
        if (isHoldExpired(clock))         throw new HoldExpiredException(holdExpiresAt);
        this.status = Status.BOOKED;
    }

    public void release(UserId user) {
        if (status == Status.BOOKED)      throw new AlreadyBookedException();
        this.status = Status.AVAILABLE; this.heldBy = null; this.holdExpiresAt = null;
    }

    public Status status() { return status; }        // reading is fine
    // no setStatus, no setHeldBy, no setHoldExpiresAt
}

Three invariants are now enforced structurally rather than by convention: you cannot be BOOKED without having been HELD; you cannot confirm someone else's hold; you cannot confirm an expired one. And the diagram of legal transitions is readable straight off the public methods, which is what makes the State-pattern refactor (→ item 18) mechanical if the interviewer asks for it.

The other half of the rule is the constructor: validate there, so an object that exists is valid. An entity that can be constructed empty and populated by setters has no moment at which it's guaranteed correct.

Failure Mode

Getters and setters generated reflexively — IDE habit, Lombok @Data, JPA muscle memory. Ask of every setter: is there a rule about when this may change? If yes, delete it and name the transition.

Enforcing the rule in the service instead. It works until the second caller. The point is that there can't be a second implementation of the rule.

Exposing mutable internals. getSeats() returning the live List lets a caller mutate the collection around your back. Return List.copyOf(...).

Connections

  • Previous: 09-law-of-demeter-tell-dont-ask.md
  • Next: 11-anemic-domain-model.md — what the absence of this looks like at scale.
  • Enables: ../04-concurrency-in-lld/27-identify-the-contended-resource.md — the intent method is the unit you lock.
  • Formalises to: ../03-design-patterns/18-state.md

notes.title: Anemic Domain Model

headings.text: Why It's the Trap for You

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • The original naming of the anti-pattern — Martin Fowler: Anemic Domain Model

Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The shape? Rich object graph, getters/setters only, all logic in a *Service.
Why is it the default failure of a Spring engineer? Years of @Entity + @Service: the entity is a row, the service is the behaviour.
The core objection? The object holds the data that defines a rule but not the rule, so every caller is a place the rule can break.
The fix, precisely? Decisions move into the entity; orchestration stays in the service.
Do you delete the service layer? No. It gets shorter.

The 30-Second Answer

An anemic model looks object-oriented — real classes, real relationships — but the objects are data holders and every behaviour lives in a service. Fowler's objection is that it takes the cost of building a domain model and none of the benefit: the rules that govern a piece of state end up outside the object that owns it, so they're duplicated, drift apart, and can be bypassed. In an LLD round it's the structural criticism most often levelled at engineers from a JPA background, and interviewers name it explicitly.

Why It's the Trap for You

Production Spring codebases often are anemic, for real reasons — ORM lifecycle constraints, transaction boundaries at the service, DTO mapping at the edges. So the habit is trained, deeply, and it transfers into the interview where those reasons don't apply.

The strongest move is to acknowledge the tension rather than pretend it doesn't exist:

"In our Spring services the entity is usually a JPA row and the logic sits in a service — transaction boundaries make that convenient. For a 60-minute in-memory design I'd put the transitions on the entity instead, because the invariant then has exactly one home and the concurrency follow-up has something to lock."

That sentence demonstrates you know both shapes and chose one, which scores far better than either the anemic design or a purist one delivered without awareness.

In Practice

// ❌ Anemic. BookingService knows ShowSeat's rules; ShowSeat knows nothing.
class ShowSeat { Status status; UserId heldBy; Instant expiry;
                 /* + get/set for all three */ }

class BookingService {
    Booking confirm(ShowSeatId id, UserId user) {
        ShowSeat s = repo.find(id);
        if (s.getStatus() != HELD) throw new IllegalStateException();
        if (!s.getHeldBy().equals(user)) throw new IllegalStateException();
        if (Instant.now().isAfter(s.getExpiry())) throw new IllegalStateException();
        s.setStatus(BOOKED);                       // and the same 4 lines in CancelService,
        return new Booking(...);                   // AdminService, ExpirySweeper...
    }
}

// ✅ Split by kind of work. The service orchestrates; the entity decides.
class BookingService {
    Booking confirm(List<ShowSeatId> ids, UserId user, String idempotencyKey) {
        return idempotency.execute(idempotencyKey, () -> {
            List<ShowSeat> seats = repo.findAllOrdered(ids);   // orchestration: which, what order
            seats.forEach(s -> s.confirm(user, clock));        // decision: inside the entity
            seats.forEach(repo::save);
            return Booking.of(seats, user, clock);
        });
    }
}

The heuristic for what goes where: a decision about one entity's own state belongs to that entity; choosing which entities, in what order, and what to do with a failure belongs to the service. Behaviour that genuinely spans entities — Splitwise debt simplification, elevator dispatch across a bank — is a domain service, which is neither anemic nor misplaced.

Failure Mode

@Data / generated accessors on domain classes. It produces the anemic shape by default, before you've made any decision.

Overcorrecting into a god entity. Pushing repository access, notification and payment into ShowSeat breaks SRP in the other direction. The entity owns its own state's rules and nothing else.

Connections

  • Previous: 10-encapsulation-of-invariants.md — the mechanical fix.
  • Next: 12-interface-segregation-for-extension-points.md
  • Cause: 09-law-of-demeter-tell-dont-ask.md

notes.title: Interface Segregation for Extension Points
notes.html:
Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Name three extension-point interfaces you'd reach for. PricingStrategy, NotificationChannel, AllocationPolicy.
What are they, functionally? The knobs the follow-up question turns.
How wide should one be? Usually one method. If implementers stub half of it, it's two interfaces.
The ISP smell? UnsupportedOperationException in an implementation.
How many in a 60-minute design? Three or four, on axes the problem statement hints at.

The 30-Second Answer

Each extension point is a narrow interface — often a single method — placed on an axis you expect to move. Narrow matters twice over: a one-method interface is trivial to implement, so the follow-up costs eight lines rather than a class full of stubs; and it can't accumulate methods that only some implementers support, which is the ISP violation.

Why It Matters

The follow-up feature is a new implementation of one of these. That's the whole mechanism by which a design "extends" (→ item 7), so the quality of the extension points is the quality of the design.

Width is the design decision. PricingStrategy { Money price(Seat, Show); } can be implemented in one expression. A PricingStrategy that also declares validateCoupon, explainBreakdown and supportsCurrency forces every new rule to answer three questions it doesn't care about, and the implementations start throwing — at which point you've built the fat interface from the ISP example (→ item 6).

In Practice

// One method each. A new rule, channel or policy is one small class.
public interface PricingRule       { Money apply(Money running, Seat seat, Show show); }
public interface NotificationChannel { void send(UserId to, Message m); }
public interface AllocationPolicy  { Optional<ParkingSpot> choose(List<ParkingSpot> free, Vehicle v); }
public interface SchedulingStrategy { Optional<Elevator> pick(List<Elevator> cars, Request r); }

// The follow-up, in full:
public final class WeekendSurcharge implements PricingRule {
    @Override public Money apply(Money running, Seat seat, Show show) {
        return show.startsOnWeekend() ? running.times(new BigDecimal("1.2")) : running;
    }
}

Composition falls out for free: PricingRule implementations chain in a list, so weekend + coupon + seat-tier compose without any of them knowing about the others. That's usually a stronger answer than a single PricingStrategy that must compute the whole price, and it's worth saying why — "rules compose, so coupon stacking is an ordering question rather than a new strategy."

Where to place them, by problem: pricing/fees (parking, booking, ride-hailing), allocation (spot, seat, driver), scheduling/dispatch (elevator, task runner), eviction (cache), split rules (Splitwise), notification transport (anything with alerts).

Failure Mode

Interfaces with no second implementation and no named future requirement. Speculative generality (→ item 26).

Fat extension interfaces. If a new implementer has to stub methods, split it.

Putting the interface on the wrong axis. Abstracting SeatRepository while leaving pricing as an if-chain, in a round whose follow-up is a pricing change. The clarifying questions (item 1) are how you avoid this.

Connections

  • Previous: 11-anemic-domain-model.md
  • Next: 13-constructor-dependency-injection.md — how the implementation gets in.
  • Why: 07-open-closed-as-the-scoring-rubric.md
  • Pattern: ../03-design-patterns/14-strategy.md

notes.title: Dependency Injection by Constructor
notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Injected time as the documented best practice — Java SE 21 API: java.time.Clock

Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The rule? No new on a collaborator inside a business class; no static singletons reached out to.
Constructor or field injection? Constructor — the dependency list is visible, and final fields mean a fully-formed object.
What does it buy that's scored? Testability. It's an explicit dimension in most LLD rubrics.
Do you need Spring? No. Plain constructors, wired by hand in main or a small factory.
What else counts as a dependency? Clock, randomness, ID generation — anything ambient the domain reaches for.

The 30-Second Answer

Business classes declare what they need in the constructor and store it in final fields. Nothing is created inside, nothing is reached for through a static. The class's dependency list is then readable in one line, it can be constructed with fakes in a test, and the strategy interfaces from item 12 have a way in.

Why It Matters

It's the D of SOLID made concrete, and it's what makes the extension points usable — an injected PricingRule list can be varied per test and per deployment; a new WeekendSurcharge() buried in a method cannot.

The testability argument is the one that scores. If there are ten minutes left and you want to write the two tests that raise the score disproportionately (→ item 41), those tests exist only if the class can be constructed with a fixed Clock and a fake repository. Design decisions made at minute ten are what make minute fifty possible.

And the Clock case is worth naming explicitly, because the Java documentation states it as the recommended practice: pass a Clock into anything that needs the current instant, with DI as the mechanism, so tests can substitute Clock.fixed or Clock.offset (→ item 38).

In Practice

public final class BookingService {
    private final ShowSeatRepository repo;
    private final PricingEngine pricing;
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    private final IdempotencyStore idempotency;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Duration holdTtl;

    public BookingService(ShowSeatRepository repo, PricingEngine pricing,
                          PaymentGateway gateway, IdempotencyStore idempotency,
                          Clock clock, Duration holdTtl) {
        this.repo = repo; this.pricing = pricing; this.gateway = gateway;
        this.idempotency = idempotency; this.clock = clock; this.holdTtl = holdTtl;
    }
    // no `new` anywhere below this line
}

// Wiring by hand — no framework needed, and it's three lines on a whiteboard.
var service = new BookingService(
        new InMemoryShowSeatRepository(),
        new PricingEngine(List.of(new SeatTierRule(), new WeekendSurcharge())),
        new FakePaymentGateway(),
        new InMemoryIdempotencyStore(),
        Clock.systemUTC(),
        Duration.ofMinutes(10));

// And the test the design above makes possible.
var service = new BookingService(repo, pricing, gateway, idem,
        Clock.fixed(T0, UTC), Duration.ofMinutes(10));

Six constructor parameters is also a signal worth reading: past about five or six, the class probably has more than one responsibility (→ item 6, SRP). Take it as a prompt to check, not as a hard limit.

Singletons. If asked, the correct Java answer is the enum singleton or the holder idiom, and the correct design answer is that a singleton reached for statically is an un-injectable dependency — which is exactly why singletons hurt testability (→ item 16).

Failure Mode

new StripeGateway() inside confirm(). Untestable and closed to a second provider — a DIP and an OCP violation in one line.

Field injection with @Autowired on a whiteboard. It hides the dependency list, allows partially-constructed objects, and imports a framework into a design that doesn't need one.

Reaching for Instant.now() in domain code. Same category of error as new: an ambient dependency the test cannot control.
